newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: PRESS DIGEST-Australian General News - April 10.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST-Australian General News - April 10.

text.p: (Compiled for Reuters by Media Monitors)
THE AUSTRALIAN FINANCIAL REVIEW

In the first stage of the Federal Government's response to the Wallis inquiry into Australia's financial system, the "six pillars" policy of prohibiting mergers of the big four banks and two largest lift insurers will be dropped. The policy removes the Treasurer's veto rights over the mergers, leaving any scrutiny to the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission. Page 1.

Australian Industrial Relations commission deputy president Ann Harrison has found that unions cannot make 'roping in' awards that seek to bind new employers to the comprehensive conditions in existing awards. The decision curtails the ability of the unions to spread comprehensive federal award regulation to new employers. Page 3.

Following the release of a report on mine safety in New South Wales by State Mineral Resources Minister Bob Martin, the New South Wales Minerals Council has denied that complacency and safety breaches occur throughout the State's mining industry. The report found that injury figures were manipulated to improve safety performance indicators. Page 4.

The Senate Department yesterday began investigating whether Independent Senator Mal Colston has, in relation to allegations of travel rorts against him, committed a serious contempt of the Senate for which he should be fined or suspended from the Parliament. Page 5.
THE AUSTRALIAN

Speaking at the release of the Wallis inquiry into Australia's financial system, Federal Treasurer Peter Costello said that the ban on mergers between the big banks will remain for now. The report recommends lifting restriction on foreign takeovers of major banks and the merging of the big insurers with banks. Page 1.

While the final Wallis report believes the cost of technology will fall and innovations in financial service will increase the ease and security of electronic transactions, the inquiry's committee members recognise that there are risks involved with the change to electronic banking. Page 1.

Controversial Independent Senator Mal Colston vowed yesterday that, despite losing support from the Federal Government in the case of the parliamentary rorts allegations against him, he would not stand down from Parliament. However, Colston has conceded e will stand down from his position as Deputy Senate President. Page 1.

Prime Minister John Howard will meet with the heads of the army, navy and air force in Sydney on Friday to discuss their concerns for sweeping reforms outlined in the defence efficiency review. The defence chiefs attacked the reforms, which they say woul strip them of their power and undermine their ability to carry out their duties of command. Page 1.
THE SYDNEY MORNING HERALD

Federal Treasurer Peter Costello yesterday released the 771-page Wallis report, saying it would deliver "enhanced competition that we believe is necessary". The report will pave the way for new competitors, including insurance companies and credit unions to fully challenge Australia's four biggest banks. Page 1.

Planned amendments to the New South Wales Mental Health Act before State Parliament would see police able to enter private homes and take people to hospital for psychiatric assessment on the advice of family members or neighbours. At present, police can only detain people for assessment if they are in a public place. Page 1.

After rejecting a statement by his staffer Christine Smith, who said she provided a false statement to explain the overclaiming of A$7,000 in travel allowances, Senator Mal Colston faces further scrutiny as the Opposition moves to exploit evidence that his abuse of parliamentary allowances extends back to the early 1980s when the Fraser Government allowed him to repay money. Page 1.

The Review of Mine Safety in NSW report has found injured NSW miners were chauffeured to work so they would sign time books, then left to spend time at home or in changing rooms so employers could cover up high injury rates. State Mineral Resources Miniser Bob Martin said the report "painted a grim picture" of mining practices in New South Wales. Page 3.
THE AGE

Independent Senator Mal Colston yesterday defied calls from the Opposition parties to quit Parliament but indicated he would resign as Deputy President of the Senate. As Colston faced increased pressure yesterday, moves were underway to strip him of much of his parliamentary superannuation payout, which could be as much as A$1.3 million. Page 1.

In a shake-up of Australia's financial services announced by Federal Treasurer Peter Costello yesterday, foreign companies will be able to take over Australian banks. While Costello ruled out a large scale takeover of Australian bank ownership to foreignbanks, he said foreign companies could knock on his door with proposals to buy into any Australian bank. Page 1.

Dr David Oberklaid, who worked at the Royal Melbourne Hospital for eight years in the occupational health program before it was privatised, resigned last week and attacked the Victorian Government and the hospital's management agreement, saying budget cut were too high and hygiene in the hospital was poor. Page 1.

Former New South Wales Liberal senator Dr Bob Woods and National Party Federal MP Michael Cobb have protested their innocence after being charged with defrauding the Commonwealth - Dr Woods under section 29D of the Crimes Act, and Cobb under sections 29D nd 29B. Both charges are in relation to alleged misuse of travel allowances and motor vehicles. Page 2.
